Red Umbrellas: First Sex Worker Pride March Organized in Boston History
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content: The marchers in front of Jacque’s, the oldest continuously operating gay bar in Boston (Andrew S) By: Andrew S BOSTON COMMON – On September 14, sex workers and allies gathered at Brewer Fountain under a canopy of red umbrellas for Boston’s historic first March for Sex Worker Pride. Led by organizers Rita Romero from Red Light Disco, Amanda Rodriguez from FemMenThem, and Jessica Van Meir from Boston Sex Workers and Allies Collective (BSWAC), the march both centered the public celebration of sex worker pride and the ongoing fight for decriminalization. Several sex workers, community organizers, and local politicians spoke to a crowd about the importance of the event before participants marched from the Common to Jacques’ Cabaret, the oldest continuously operating gay bar in the city. Speakers at the rally spoke on decriminalization, the importance of protecting bodily autonomy, and the contributions sex workers have made to the feminist and queer rights movements. The march was the first in Boston history, creating an opportunity to publicly recognize sex workers and their allies. Save Our Selves (SOS), Sex Worker Pride Boston, and Protect Trans Futures were all crucial supporters of the event. For some participants like Savannah Sly, the march marked a huge milestone: I have been a sex worker since 2003, and I am so ecstatic to see sex workers and allies visibly marching through Boston and demanding our rights be respected. I wish something like this existed when I was eighteen and was first getting started. Members of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and the Communist Party, USA (CPUSA) in attendance supported the same. Rat, co-chair of Southern New Hampshire CPUSA chapter, said: This is another step toward destigmatization, decriminalization, and collective liberation, and to be recognized for who we are in public. A red umbrella, decorated with both the political goals of the movement and aesthetics (Andrew S) Decriminalization vs. The Nordic Model The question of decriminalization has long been a battleground of policy for sex workers. One side favors the Nordic Model (also known as “end-demand”), where prostitution is a phenomenon manufactured from societal gender inequality, understanding buyers in the sex trade as the main culprit. Nordic Model organizations seek to illegalize commercial sex trade from the consumer side by targeting “Johns,” or customers of sex workers who are customarily presumed to be men. Nordic Model supporters believe that if the consumption of the commercial sex trade is made illegal, trafficking in the trade and the exploitation within the industry will effectively diminish. But advocates for full sex work decriminalization actively see the Nordic Model as a dangerous misstep that leads to more restriction on sex workers. Case studies of legalization have typically resulted in more restrictions of sex workers than protections, as the government requires sex workers to register within rigid regulations. The Nordic Model has likewise proven to restrict health care access in places like Canada , greatly increasing the number of health issues that sex workers there suffered as a result. Organizations such as the ACLU and Human Rights Watch have advocated for full decriminalization of sex work. Protection of sex workers’ right to bodily autonomy was a center pillar for many in attendance at Boston’s first Sex Worker Pride March. Beyond keeping them safe from wrongful discrimination or safety in their profession, autonomy plays an inevitable role in sex worker earnings, too. Zachary Flynn, a sex worker in the area, spoke on his own experience: In late-stage capitalism, autonomy is important. If you would rather judge someone for sex work than pay them a livable wage, then what else do you expect us to do? I work three to four jobs on top of sex work, and that is barely keeping me afloat. Zachary continued, speaking on how sex work builds wealth through labor: I think the fact that even with sex work being one of three to four jobs someone can have and even then not being able to support themselves financially says a lot on its own, but not everyone’s story with sex work is strictly about survival. It’s a chosen (and needed) profession for a fair amount of society. The point of the march is autonomy. All forms of work are selling your mind or body through means of labor, so why is it different in this context? If you have ever watched or rented porn, visited a strip club or advocated for women/queer rights, that means you support sex work, whether you realize it or not. Protect Trans Futures’ contingent marching along the Boston Common (Andrew S) From Origins to Pride Carol Leigh was the first to coin the term “sex work” in the 1980s to provide a term that described work different from prositution. According to Mary Carol of the Boston Sex Workers and Allies Collective (BSWAC), an important part of that was the emphasis on work and labor. BSWAC organized around the community around this foundational concept in the run-up to the Pride March. On September 7, BSWAC hosted a screening and panel on Working Girls (1986), independent filmmaker Lizzie Borden’s movie about a day in the life of a woman working in a brothel in New York City. An overbearing manager forces her to stay beyond her hours, while displaying glimpses of interaction between workers and clients throughout the entire day. Working Girls is a representation of sex workers and their connection to labor in the view of Mary Carol. The Pride March also took the time to remember what sex workers have contributed to and suffered historically. The red umbrellas ubiquitous across the march were not coincidence, but rather the universal symbol of solidarity that has called attention to poor working conditions faced by sex workers since 2001. Further, sex workers’ contributions far outdate the symbol. Sly stated: Sex workers helped start Pride. Sex workers are in the canaries in the coal mine for how people are treated. They are at the forefront at the advancement of human rights and bringing home the bacon for their communities at the same time. Pride is sex workers claiming their own unique space and being the focus for collective liberation. Many steps remain to make in order for sex worker pride to be fully enjoyed. Rat claimed that more needs to be done legislatively and culturally: “we need to challenge elected officials on their decriminalization stance, and we need people to speak up for sex workers even when they’re not in the room.” BSWAC’s Legislative Priorities include legislation for full decriminalization, safe reporting, and mechanisms to protect workers from sexual assault by cops. Andrew S is a member of Boston DSA and associate editor of Working Mass. The post Red Umbrellas: First Sex Worker Pride March Organized in Boston History appeared first on Working Mass .

articles.title: Brazil’s Presidential Election Is Going Down to the Wire
articles.author: Olavo Passos de Souza
articles.content: As the Brazilian presidential election on October 4 draws closer, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is in a very tight contest with Flávio Bolsonaro, the son and heir of the Bolsonaro political dynasty. Lula is leading most of the polls for the first round, but the race appears too close to call in the event of a runoff between them. This election does not merely pit two opposing candidates against each other. It is a struggle between Brazil’s democratic forces and the return to power of a reactionary bloc. Lula’s Challenge Lula is seeking a fourth term as president at the age of eighty-one. The Brazilian constitution allows for this: it does not impose any limits on how long one person can be in office, so long as they do not serve more than two consecutive terms. After his first victory in 2002, Lula went on to complete two highly successful terms. His government lifted millions out of poverty with social programs like Bolsa Familia , greatly expanded Brazil’s education and health care systems, and achieved some notable diplomatic victories at the United Nations. When he left office in 2010 with an 87 percent approval rating, most people assumed that this would mark the departure of the man Barack Obama described as the most popular politician on earth from the political scene. However, the failure of his successor Dilma Rousseff to deal with a hostile Congress, endemic corruption, and Brazil’s economic slowdown led to her impeachment — which many refer to as a soft coup — in 2016. Lula was prepared to run again in the 2018 presidential election, but the Lavo Jato (“car wash”) corruption inquiry resulted in his arrest on charges of corruption. With Lula barred from running, the far-right candidate Jair Bolsonaro defeated his Workers’ Party (PT) ally Fernando Haddad and became president. The magistrate Sergio Moro, the main figure behind Lavo Jato, soon accepted a position in Bolsonaro’s government. When further revelations discredited the investigation against Lula and revealed its chief enforcer Moro to be profoundly biased, the Supreme Court annulled his sentence and he was released. He went on to win the 2022 election after four disastrous years of Bolsonaro’s presidency before fending off a coup attempt by his vanquished opponent. Bolsonaro is now in jail because of his role in the failed coup and prohibited from seeking political office. Four years after his triumphal (some would say messianic) return to the front of the political stage, Lula’s government only has lukewarm achievements to its credit — in large part due to a hostile Congress — and it has failed to adapt to the age of social media. Lula is a figure rooted in a now bygone age of struggle for democracy during the 1970s and ’80s who reached his pinnacle in the civil and democratic 2000s. His greatest appeal at present derives from his status as the sole defender of democracy in an extremely polarized 2020s Brazil that is rife with disinformation. Bolsonaro 2.0 This amounts to a tepid appeal that is not enough for many younger voters — opposition to the far right can only carry a politician so far. Flávio Bolsonaro, who is more civilized in style but no less vile in substance than his father, has the evangelical right firmly behind him. He also has the backing of many figures within Brazil’s financial system, not to mention open support from the United States. His brother Eduardo, who is based in Florida, is almost single-handedly responsible for urging Donald Trump to impose tariffs on Brazil. Bolsonaro has suffered from a series of scandals that resulted in the viability of his candidacy being called into question just a few months ago. He was implicated in a major financial scandal with a bizarre twist, having asked a corrupt banker to finance a biographical film about his father (starring Jim Caviezel of The Passion of the Christ as Jair), Bolsonaro also fell out with his stepmother Michelle, who is herself a powerful figure among evangelicals. None of this has deterred him from carrying on, and he has bounced back in the polls with a vengeance over the course of September. This in no small part due to the fact that Alexandre de Moraes, one of Brazil’s chief jurists and a hate figure for the Bolsonarist right, has been embroiled in a corruption scandal of his own. This supplied ammunition to the Bolsonarist camp. In the event of a runoff election between Flávio and Lula, the former will be expecting to win over most of those who voted for the other candidates in the first round. All of those candidates are right-wingers of one kind or another, and the Bolsonaro camp appeals to their base far more than Lula does. In fact, they neatly represent the spectrum of the Brazilian right, with each laying claim to their own niche. The Miscellaneous Right Romeu Zema, governor of Minas Gerais, is the candidate (and only noteworthy member) of NOVO, the New Party. This is a libertarian, faux-technocratic party that promises to cut back on government excesses and do away with the corrupt state machinery. In practice, this would mean privatizing all social services and dismantling state institutions before selling them to the highest bidder. The traditional neoliberal political forces in Brazil have collapsed in the face of the Bolsonarist far right, so Zema is now the closest thing the country has to that old style of politics. His disastrous tenure in Minas Gerais, where the state debt skyrocketed during his time as governor, tells us all we need to know about his approach to managing a government. Ronaldo Caiado, governor of Goiás, is a representative of the traditional Brazilian Centrão, the “Big Center” — that is, the large, nonideological, profit-based section of Congress composed of figures who care only about preserving their own power, regardless of political positioning or policy. As governor of Goiás in the midwest, Caiado is extensively connected to Brazil’s agribusiness bloc. This bloc comprises a handful of large landowners whose properties often dwarf small countries in acreage, and who are determined to go on clearing rainforest so they can claim new land. The agribusiness bloc is one of Brazil’s most powerful lobbies, and it is squarely opposed to Lula’s environmental protection policies. Renan Santos is the political chief of the Free Brazil Movement, a reactionary, Tea Party–style movement that emerged in the early 2010s. It preaches libertarianism, demonizes anything left wing, and argues for “free speech at all costs.” The movement is heavily composed of dissatisfied young Brazilians, many of whom belong to online subcultures such as the “manosphere.” They are hostile not only to the current Brazilian state but also to many of its democratic institutions. Santos comes out with fiery rhetoric: at a debate held in August, which neither Lula nor Flavio attended, he cursed and insulted both of the leading candidates. His crypto-fascistic stances, his speeches, and his personality bring back memories of Jair Bolsonaro. However, whereas the former was a reactionary harking back to the 1960s dictatorship, Santos looked forward to a more social-media-savvy, anti-democratic future under the specter of anti-statist tech magnates such as Elon Musk and Peter Thiel. Capitalist Minds The most curious figure among the lesser candidates is the best-selling author Augusto Cury, whose self-help book and highly questionable positions on psychology have made him a rich man. Cury presents himself as a centrist candidate with a “capitalist mind and a social heart,” and is at best unclear about any major policy or position. Cury managed to reach third place in the polls, albeit with a meager 11 percent, for a few days in early September, in the midst of Flávio Bolsonaro’s many scandals, before falling back to 6 percent. Not as radioactive to left-wing and middle-ground voters as the other candidates but firmly separate from Lula and the traditional Left, Cury is the quintessential “independent” candidate. None of these candidates poll much higher than 5 percent, and all of them draw support from segments of conservative Brazilians who are frightened of Bolsonaro but will take any alternative to Lula. Lula is unquestionably a political and electoral titan, but he has not produced a successor or replacement who could give the sense that there is a younger generation coming forward in Brazilian politics. Dilma Rousseff now serves as president of the World Development Bank, while Fernando Haddad has been tainted by multiple defeats. Flávio Dino, the former governor of Maranhão, was a popular and charismatic figure, but Lula nominated him to serve on the Brazilian Supreme Court in 2024, which removed him from the political scene. Instead of grooming a replacement for 2026, Lula chose to run for a fourth term, which pits him against a much younger option. The results of the upcoming election will reveal whether this proves to be a bridge too far in his long career.

articles.title: Amazon Is Perfecting Total Surveillance of Its Workforce
articles.author: C. R. Calabria
articles.content: Although Amazon is increasingly synonymous with worker surveillance , the logistics behemoth has never been a pioneer in that space. UPS was the first fleet to install GPS in their vehicles back in 1991. Netradyne, the company that makes the AI-powered product Driver.i installed in most vehicles in Amazon’s fleet, had already logged over a hundred million minutes of driving time before Amazon signed the firm on. But with each new iteration of its delivery-aid-cum-surveillance tech, Amazon has proven its knack for taking an existing product and deploying it in a dystopian direction. And other companies tend to follow its lead. “Smart delivery glasses,” Amazon’s latest gadgets, which come with a specialized vest with a built-in battery-pack, were introduced on their in-house news site last October to little fanfare ; only a couple of niche tech websites covered it. According to a recent post on r/AmazonDSPDrivers, a Reddit community for Amazon’s scattered global network of Delivery Service Partner (DSP) drivers, training with the smart glasses at some DSPs has begun. It’s not unlikely that a nationwide rollout may come as soon as this year’s holiday season. On the surface, the aim of smart delivery glasses is to replace the use of the smartphone on the job, allowing the driver to pay attention to their surroundings instead of looking at their phone. For DSP drivers, the smartphone is everything: It identifies packages, provides a walking path from the vehicle to the delivery location, instructs drivers on where and how to deliver items, photographs packages at the designated drop-off location, and requires a swipe to confirm completion of a delivery. With smart delivery glasses, Amazon promises to make delivering “safer and more seamless,” which is very likely true — I imagine, as a former DSP driver myself, that at least they will make it less annoying to sort through an overpacked cargo area. But the smart glasses reflect a larger philosophical position, one ubiquitous in Big Tech and fueled by the artificial intelligence gold rush: that the human is not enough, and that we need to be aided — and disciplined — by AI. A Formidable Surveillance Arsenal Each device in Amazon’s surveillance arsenal serves a unique function. The Amazon app tracks a driver’s location and pace in real time, sending that information to Amazon and the driver’s DSP. Then comes Driver.i. With one camera pointed at the road, one camera at the driver, and two side-view cameras, the platform records drivers at all times, analyzing 100 percent of driving time. When an infraction occurs — whether an actual infraction or one that Driver.i has made up — the Driver.i robot scolds you in real time, sending video of your alleged infraction to Amazon, to you, and to your DSP. Right now, the surveillance stops there. But with the introduction of smart delivery glasses, surveillance never has to end. Put your delivery vehicle in park, and the glasses automatically turn on. Like Alejandro Jodorowsky’s sketches of his never-created Dune , the latest technology is Amazon’s mad vision come to life: the ouroboros of watching people at work. Amazon’s model is more than surveillance. At the core of its vision, Amazon is doing what it has always done best: both spearheading and reflecting the worst antihuman impulses of our age. Its proliferation is the result of what David Moscrop calls our “ shared pastureland ” breaking. Ring cameras, for one, have been a subsidiary of Amazon since 2018; the desire to protect one’s packages from would-be thieves prompts many people to purchase Ring cameras. Last year, Ring announced a partnership with Flock Safety, the increasingly maligned surveillance company, which was canceled this February after a public backlash over a Super Bowl ad. (Flock has an entire page dedicated to how it serves Amazon.) Isolation is central to both the consumer and employee experiences. Amazon, which does not directly hire any of the hundreds of thousands of workers who deliver its packages, nevertheless pays millions of dollars yearly to union-busting consulting firms to ensure workers’ isolation, claiming that its tactics are protected by the First Amendment. Just last year, Amazon fired 150 workers who had organized with a Queens-based DSP. The year before, eighty-four workers at a DSP in Palmdale, California, successfully negotiated a union contract with its DSP; the DSP’s contract with Amazon was quickly terminated. And when workers in Quebec unionized a warehouse, the company responded by shutting down its operations across the whole province. Not only does Amazon use technology to push humans to the limits of their productive capacity at work, but it also creates tandem machine-human systems that encourage humans to become nonthinking bodies: isolated and automated. Every critical decision, from deciding how many workers will deliver in a given day (a common DSP practice is to schedule more workers than it needs, waiting for the algorithm to decide how many it can put into vehicles), to configuring routes, to punishing driving infractions, is configured by an automated AI system. For example: If the AI decides you’ve run a red light, and you can’t prove you didn’t, it’s an immediate termination. A Human Future for Work? Amazon’s plan to surveil and automate work at every step is a vision mid-implementation. The logical end point of this AI-driven efficiency is pure automation: in other words, brainlessness. The last stop of ultimate efficiency is what some people might call animal, and others might call lobotomized. Both terms gesture toward the same thing: at best, that human workers are too slow, and at worst, that human workers are not to be trusted. The source of this tendency is, of course, the long-standing capitalist goal of asserting ever-greater control over workers and replacing them entirely where possible. UPS workers, who are unionized, have demonstrated an alternate vision for the future of work. When UPS decided to install its own Lytx DriveCam monitoring system in 2022 (followed shortly thereafter by FedEx and Walmart), the Teamsters union disputed the use of the technology, claiming that it infringed on workers’ rights. What workers and the company eventually settled on was to record only when a driving infraction was detected, such as a vehicle swerving or impact, to protect the driver as much as to surveil them. To evaluate the difference between each technology, you might ask: When a new AI-first technology is implemented, does the technology actually aim to make drivers safer — giving them more protection in the event of an accident? Or is its point to punish drivers by using negative reinforcement to curb bad driving habits? You might then look at how the implementation of the technology aligns with the company’s long-term vision. For instance: Is the point of technology like Driver.i — whose creator Netradyne began with self-driving aspirations — to make the driver safe, or to ultimately make the driver obsolete? Despite our moral qualms with these labor practices, Americans can’t seem to get over using Amazon. When I worked for a DSP last summer because I was desperate (and it was one of the better-paying jobs in the area), I felt a little like my Amazon job was penance for all of the Amazon shopping that I had done over the years: for all of the delivery drivers who had come to my various houses and apartments in the extreme heat and cold; who hadn’t had a break in ten hours; who had nowhere to pee. Yet there’s no fundamental reason why efficient package delivery needs to involve dehumanizing surveillance, AI discipline, and otherwise degrading labor conditions. The unionized UPS drivers who have successfully fought back against surveillance, and the growing efforts to organize Amazon itself, point to the possibility of a more human future for work, one where collective action limits management’s ability to spy on and control its workforce.

articles.title: Primetime Turns Chris Hansen Into a Horror Show
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content: Primetime has an interesting look that’s the key to its worldview, which is that our society is so bad that no one can escape its infecting qualities. There’s a smeary effect around the edge of the lens in many shots, which are generally in shallow focus, making everything appear greasy and defiled and half-hidden. This is in addition to a lurid color scheme dominated by nasty shades of red, green, and blue that are often clashing with each other, so that characters’ faces emerge out of surroundings that seem disgustingly tainted. Robert Pattinson, playing Chris Hansen — the real-life former host of the hit NBC Dateline series To Catch a Predator that ran from 2004 to 2007 — appears in certain close-ups with his face suffused in an unwholesome tint of hellfire red. Appropriately enough, much of the film was shot with an actual colonoscopy camera. Hansen is portrayed as a self-deluding creep who ultimately gets less sympathy than the entrapped pedophiles. At some level, it seems, Hansen knows how rotten he is. In an early scene, when he’s in the first-class section on an airplane with a seatmate who’s a big fan of the show, he quickly warms to all the praise. He starts to confide in the sadistic old man, who ultimately wants to know: Doesn’t Hansen want to personally beat up the sexual predators he puts on camera? “Don’t you want to make them bleed?” he asks in a hideous close-up. And Hansen brags, with a horrible shit-eating grin, that actually, “I think what we do might be even worse.” Primetime is the first narrative feature film directed by Lance Oppenheim, who’s best known for the HBO documentary series Ren Faire . Oppenheim had an incredible twofer triumph at film festival premieres earlier this month, as Primetime garnered enormous attention at the Venice International Film Festival while the Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything , which Oppenheim codirected with Nathan Fielder, created a sensation at the Telluride Film Festival. Both films portray a person being studied in endless close-ups who represents a bottomless pit of social corruption, and both films were shot with approximately the same crew, including David Bolen, who’s long been Oppenheim’s chosen director of photography. You Can See Everything doesn’t open in theaters until October 16, but its signature shot is already iconic and widely memed . It’s a long-held close-up of the appallingly blank, infantile face of blue-eyed blonde businesswoman Elizabeth Holmes. Those baby-blues are wide open and unblinking in the film’s preview as she says over and over that she’s “being real” and telling the truth about her health technology company Theranos, through which Holmes was then committing fraud on a vast scale. She’s now serving an eleven-year prison sentence. Corruption in Close-Up Primetime also spends a lot of time contemplating faces in close-up. There’s Pattinson’s face representing Hansen as all sharp vulpine lines, slit-eyed, hungry, and almost feral when he thinks he’s unobserved. There’s the smushier, harder-to-read face of his show’s producer, Andie Bender (Merritt Wever), who occasionally ponders her own limitless indifference to morality or the well-being of others right before sliding back into producer mode, cracking the whip or smoothly shifting over into soft, specious persuasion in order to keep the show running as a ratings winner. And then there’s Dan Plum (Skyler Gisondo), the aspiring actor and naive new recruit who’s at the center of the show’s sting operations. His youthful, freckle-faced appearance and golly-gee manner are considered perfect for a twenty-three-year-old actor who needs to play an eager thirteen-year-old boy inviting pedophiles over to his house for sex while his parents are away. Dan Plum really wants a professional credit that’ll get him a Screen Actors’ Guild card. What he’ll actually get is something far more unsettling. In Primetime , a lurid color scheme dominated by nasty shades of red, green, and blue that are often clashing with each other makes characters’ faces emerge out of surroundings that seem disgustingly tainted. (A24) But he stays on To Catch a Predator — even after giving that first ad-libbed “performance” that gets a little too real as he registers shock and fear at the sudden display of whipped-cream-slathered genitals by a young male predator in a hurry. He stays on the show partly because of hero-worship, as he’s lured in by the phony mentoring offered by Chris Hansen. Hansen cynically nicknames him “Decoy Dan” and persuades him that his awesome acting skills are doing the Lord’s work, saving innocent children. Meanwhile, Hansen’s marriage is unraveling. He’s giving his wife Mary Joan Hansen (Anna Faris) extravagant promises to reform even as he’s doubling down on his career and cheating on her with another woman. A National Enquirer photographer snaps a compromising photo of Hansen and the girlfriend even as she’s becoming an ex-girlfriend, and the blackmailing threats kick in as soon as To Catch a Predator gets abruptly moved into prime time by a network executive who smells an opportunity. This sudden white-hot chance to achieve mainstream success, which is immediately imperiled, pushes Hansen, producer Andie Bender, and Dan Plum over the edge into very dark terrain. Robert Pattinson is not just the star of Primetime , he’s also a producer on the movie and was the one to bring the Ajon Singh script, based on the 2009 Esquire article “Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die,” to Oppenheim. Though his performance is divisive, it’s so startling and so dominates the film, that he’s considered a leading contender for essentially every award nomination this season. Pattinson’s Talent and Star Power Personally, I love the way Pattinson is going for more extreme and stylized effects reminiscent of old-time Hollywood actors. My podcasting partner noted that Pattinson’s waspish performance of villainy in The Odyssey , as the most malevolent of the suitors bedeviling Penelope, shows him moving into “Roddy McDowall mode.” McDowall, a brilliantly gifted child star in the golden age of the studio system, became a character actor as an adult and created a memorable rogues’ gallery of amusingly twisted and sinister figures, all colorfully portrayed right to the edge of camp and occasionally well over it. Today, giving such a performance is a high-risk move to make in any modern “prestige” film offering, all due to an infatuation with method acting that began back in the 1950s. It was in this era that “going method” first convinced critics and audiences that there’s no other way to give a good performance than in this one style, generally termed the most “realistic.” There are, of course, many acting styles — Delsarte, Brechtian, Expressionistic, etc. — but the critical knives are out for anything but the Americanized, Konstantin Stanislavsky–influenced “method” performances that took over most acting schools generations ago. The most famous example of a divisive non-method performance is probably Jack Nicholson’s harrowing, ultrastylized tour de force in The Shining (1980), which director Stanley Kubrick intended as an opposing force to Shelley Duvall’s wrung-out naturalism. As Nicholson put it , actors shouldn’t have just “one set of theories.” For him, it all depended on the film in question. “You can go for years saying, ‘I’m gonna get this thing real because they really haven’t seen it real’ [. . . . ] and then you come up against someone like Stanley [Kubrick] who says, ‘Yeah, it’s real, but it’s not interesting.’” Say what you will, Pattinson is definitely interesting here, going for effects that wouldn’t be out of place in an old-school gothic horror film. But he’s entirely in key with the sensational punch Oppenheim is going for: redefining the possibilities of the biopic genre with this “fever dream” that captures “an emotional truth.” As Oppenheim puts it, “When you spend a lot of time doing reportage on an extremely dark subject, it must rub off on you. Rob [Pattinson] and I watched [Chris Hansen] on Theo Von’s podcast, and Theo asked how he deals with all the darkness. He said, ‘I just bury it deep down inside.’ That was a really telling answer.” While Primetime is playing in theaters, the real-life Chris Hansen is making the rounds to express his criticisms of the film, which he claims is “a hit piece” that’s “98% . . . pure fiction.” On the Fox News show Jesse Watters Primetime , Hansen presented footage of himself actually attending the film in a Times Square theater in New York City. On his way in, he notes that Lance Oppenheim contacted him late in production and told him the film was “a love letter to Chris Hansen,” giving Hansen the perfect setup for his punch line, “If that was a love letter, I’d hate to get a poison pen letter.” After seeing the film, Hansen — ever the showman — interviewed other audience members emerging from the theater who express support for Hansen as well as Hansen’s own view of his show To Catch a Predator ’s legacy: “All we do is expose bad human beings who try to hurt children.” Of course, Oppenheim is positively gleeful about Hansen’s response to Primetime : His reaction to the film right now is exactly what the film is about. I was a fan of Chris Hansen, and I still am. That’s why I wanted to make this film. Yes, he’s a journalist. Yes, he’s an entertainer. But he’s also an artist. He made this hall of mirrors, with adult actors pretending to be children and sets that look like something out of Blue Velvet . . . . To me, he’s a hero, a complicated hero. . . . He’s a human with flaws setting out to do something noble, and the effects of capitalism and commercialism make for a confusing experience for him. Somewhat incredibly, Oppenheim insists that he has no intention of villainizing Hansen, even as he explores the sadistic thrills built into “performative justice,” updated for the mass media and the always-online age. There are other kinds of predation involved here, dating back to the days of “the whipping post, the pillory, the town whipper that would show up and publicly lash a criminal and thousands of people in the town square would turn up to watch. Chris Hansen is the new version of that guy.” If the film has a message, it’s not a complicated one — the point is that certain terrible things shouldn’t be staged, marketed, and exhibited for public entertainment, because that process has a dark and degrading effect on everyone involved. We don’t have public hangings anymore for a reason. Yet it’s remarkable how, in interviews with Hansen expressing his utter inability to comprehend what Oppenheim thinks he’s doing in Primetime — even after quoting Oppenheim’s own explanations — he’s got that same wide-eyed, unblinking, uncomprehending expression of blank-faced innocence as Elizabeth Holmes. With Primetime and — very soon — the much anticipated Holmes documentary, Oppenheim is undeniably an artist for our times.

articles.title: Economic Democracy Is at the Heart of Socialism
articles.author: Mike Beggs
articles.content: In 1872, British courts prosecuted more than seventeen thousand workers for a single offense: leaving their jobs. Under the Master and Servants Acts, wage laborers who quit before the end of an agreed term, or who merely refused to show up to work, could be sentenced to three months of hard labor. Employers who violated the same rule, by withholding wages or firing someone without notice, owed just a civil debt. Across the 1860s and early 1870s, as the labor market tightened and approached full employment, the number of prosecutions rose. Even before the eight-hour day became one of organized labor’s defining demands, one of the British trade union movement’s earliest sustained legislative campaigns was to end the criminal punishment of workers who left their jobs. They finally won that right in 1875, when workers were finally allowed to sell their time and withdraw at will, coerced though they still were by the mute compulsion of economic relations. Today even socialist critics of capitalism count the freedom to leave a job as one of the basic liberties that separates a wage earner from a serf. But we need to demand more. Decisions about labor discipline, the pace of work, shift length, and how the proceeds are divvied up belong unambiguously to workers. While past struggles secured us the freedom of exit, the freedom to not be jailed for simply walking out of our workplaces, it left untouched the question of who rules within them when we have no choice but to stay. The Realities of Capitalist Labor Markets At the site of extraction, the boss rules like a dictator. Labor unions and the regulatory state sanded off some of the roughest edges of workplace tyranny, but the forces of capitalist innovation generate creative ways to restore those edges every day. There’s a reason why workers at Amazon warehouses race to fulfill their quotas in an atmosphere of electronic surveillance and skip bathroom breaks for fear of falling behind. Short of disrupting the system through collective action, the only shred of control workers have under capitalism is the power of exit. Even when workers are in a position to exercise it, though, the power of exit has serious limitations. For one thing, workers can’t exercise this leverage often — your future job prospects suffer if there are too many gaps in your employment history. For another, in most cases, it’s far easier for a company to replace one of its workers than for the worker to replace the source of their livelihood. Things are a bit different for those workers whose skills are particularly desired by employers, but supply and demand work much the same way in the labor market as they do in any other market — rare skills confer more bargaining power precisely because they are rare. For most workers, most of the time, wage labor in what we can think of as its “natural state” is a take-it-or-leave-it proposition. Workers whose only freedom is the freedom of exit can decide which particular capitalist dominates them, but they still can’t fully control their own lives. Labor contracts cannot provide a fully enforceable promise of what employers want to pay for. The contract is for time spent under the direction of the employer. The wage pays for time, but the employer is ultimately interested in the results of an employee’s work, which depend also on the employee’s ability and effort over the time for which they are employed. But usually neither effort nor ability is fully observable; monitoring them is costly, and the firm cannot rely on external legal enforcement. This makes employment a contested exchange, as economists Samuel Bowles and Herbert Gintis put it. For various reasons, the results of employment cannot be contracted for explicitly, especially because much production is done by teams, often involving heterogeneous tasks, and it is difficult to identify the contribution of individuals. (Piecework and independent contracting are exceptions, but these arrangements are impossible in many fields.) Level of effort cannot be contracted for in an enforceable way either — it is even more difficult to observe. What can be contracted for is time at work, under the direction of the employer, within the parameters of a job description. This matters to the question of whether workers can effectively express their preferences about working conditions on the labor market. It means that much about work is not determined, and so not fully priced, at the point of transaction. It is bargained for among parties already in a contractual relationship — sometimes formally, but more often informally and from day to day. It plays out in employer decisions about how to monitor, discipline, and motivate employees as well as employee decisions about how to work in response. Terminating the contract is a move both can play in this game, and the possibility hangs over the bargain. This brings the state of the labor market back into the picture: general conditions of supply and demand for labor affect people’s willingness to take the exit option. But crucially, the labor market generally does not clear, and labor is usually on the long side of the market — that is, supply of labor typically exceeds demand at going rates of pay. Unemployment is a perennial feature of capitalism. If a worker can expect to quickly find an equivalent job at their current salary and conditions, the risk of job loss does not have much sting. But workers usually face much more uncertainty than that. Many may be reasonably confident about being able to find some work while being very nervous about finding a job that matches their current pay and conditions. This makes the exit option costly and gives management an upper hand in negotiations about how work is to be done. How employers use this advantage varies across jobs. They have to deal with the fact that they have paid for people’s time, and that those people are not robots or tools. Employees still have to be motivated to work. In some jobs, a monitor-and-discipline approach works. The employer keeps tight surveillance over the production process or its results and threatens dismissal if the worker does not meet the benchmarks. Amazon warehouse and delivery tracking systems are a pure example, but this strategy has a long history in factories everywhere. Many jobs, however, are not as easy to monitor. Here employers depend on some amount of internal worker motivation, which tends to be undermined by aggressive surveillance and discipline. High employee turnover is costly to employers too — it takes time to train new workers and replace lost experience. Employers are especially loath to lose their most productive employees, even if it is not always easy to identify who they are. Since it is exactly these employees that are most likely to feel confident about finding work elsewhere, employers try to make sure they have something to lose. Most employers therefore use some combination of carrot and stick, the arts of the human resources department: performance reviews with the possibility of both promotion ladders and disciplinary measures. We Need Workplace Democracy Workplace democracy is not in itself an alternative to the labor market; it supplements the right of exit with a voice within the firm. Exit is not enough, not only because of the limited practical freedom people often have to leave a job or to be picky about job offers but also because the cooperative nature of production makes colleagues’ preferences about work highly interdependent with one another. They cannot be accommodated in the same way as individual consumer preferences. Cooperative work needs to be coordinated: for example, in many jobs people have to be on shift at the same time. Someone must coordinate a team process. But without an effective way for workers to voice their preferences and have those preferences be taken into account, the coordination will happen on the employer’s terms. Workers can only express objections in negative ways: by leaving, by quietly not cooperating, by working less diligently and energetically than they might. At best, collective bargaining through a union gives workers a seat at the table, but they are still usually restricted to responding defensively to employer initiative. In contrast, in a democratic workplace, administrators are accountable to their colleagues. Not only must worker preferences be taken into account, but they must be actively sought. Those preferences can now be expressed positively, with those working together also working out together how best to do the job. Liberal philosophy typically excludes the workplace from its arguments for democracy on the grounds that it is part of a zone of voluntary exchange in which individuals are best able to freely pursue their own interests. But, as discussed above, because of unemployment, the boss finds any individual worker replaceable, whereas the individual worker cannot be sure of finding an alternative buyer for their labor power at the going wage at will. And even in conditions of full employment, a worker switching jobs is still incurring far more dislocation and inconvenience than a consumer changing purchasing habits. Because there is a relation of power rather than a relation of free and equal exchange, even considerations of liberal political justice can be used to argue that the power should be accountable to those over whom it is exercised. Workers are not inert “inputs” but agents with wills of their own, conscious subjects whose experiences and wishes should be taken into account. Liberal arguments for democracy in the political sphere apply also to the firm. Bowles and Gintis draw on political theorist Robert Dahl’s observation that “exit” from a firm is often so costly that membership is, for all practical purposes, compulsory. When leaving one’s job entails serious loss of income and stability, the government of a firm begins to resemble the government of a state: because exit is costly, membership is not significantly more voluntary than citizenship in a country. In that sense, the same democratic principles that justify accountability in political life can be extended to economic life as well. How Would Workplace Democracy Actually Work? In a socialist economic order where democracy had been extended to the workplace, there could be a wide plurality of specific firm constitutions, but the standard for a midsize to large firm would involve representative democracy, with elected directors appointing and monitoring administrators who would be responsible for day-to-day management. This could be supplemented by committees and referenda as needed, but routine administration is best handled by specialist professional workers with expertise in accounting, logistics, and so on. Democracy does its job by making sure the administrators are ultimately answerable to their colleagues and that working conditions and broad questions of strategy have general approval. In a fundamental way, democratic firms are very different from capitalist ones. Capitalist firms are ultimately controlled by their owners, who are also the claimants to the residual income left after suppliers, workers, and creditors have been paid. Labor-managed firms, on the other hand, are ultimately controlled by their workers. Worker-members receive two forms of income from their firms. They earn a regular wage, fixed in advance, and a periodic dividend, their share of the firm’s profit. There is no way of efficiently maintaining a complex division of labor that would guarantee everyone their dream job. In a democratic firm, membership in a workplace and appointment to specific roles both involve agreement of the worker and the democratic organization itself. Worker-members are free to leave but not to be automatically accepted in a role elsewhere. Democracy at work would have to be, and we’re confident it will be, economically viable too. People would have little reason to embrace a system that gave them more say but left them unable to meet their needs. Efficiency in the economic sense is broader than technical efficiency in turning inputs into outputs. It is not necessary for our argument that cooperative firms outperform nondemocratic firms in productivity. Other advantages may make up for some deficiencies in productivity. Workers may prefer less pressure on the job to higher income but be unable to effectively express such preferences in capitalist conditions. However, it is important that labor-managed firms are at least reasonably productive. If workplace democracy came at too high a price in terms of real income, the claim for economic efficiency in the broader sense would be shakier. Empirical evidence offers little support for the idea that democratic workplaces are inherently inefficient. Cooperative firms perform at least as well as conventional ones in productivity and survival, and often better. As economist Gregory Dow notes, real labor-managed firms do not conform to the familiar caricature of chaos: Their members generally do not shirk work, fight over wages, or rebel against supervisors, nor do such firms quickly collapse or drift back into capitalist control. They manage to coordinate production and maintain discipline without replicating the coercion of capitalist management. Of course, we should be cautious about generalizing too far from these findings, since they come from cooperatives operating within capitalist markets. Even so, the evidence sharply undermines the intuition that only authoritarian management can make production work. The intuition that democratic firms must be less disciplined than their traditional peers rests on the idea that participation will weaken managerial authority and lower effort. Bowles and Gintis point instead to several mechanisms that can raise productivity. Democracy obliges management to consider the social costs of supervision and the pace of work. While democratic firms still rely on monitoring and incentives, these must win broad consent and so tend to be less arbitrary and more legitimate. Legitimacy makes work less alienating and morale higher — conditions usually associated with better performance. Workers are also better placed than managers to gauge one another’s effort. Peer pressure and pride in shared achievement can do more to sustain discipline than orders from above, since slacking off harms colleagues rather than distant owners. Profit sharing adds another spur: when returns go to the workforce, each member has a tangible stake in the firm’s results. The effect weakens as enterprises grow larger, but even then measures to improve efficiency are easier to support when their benefits flow to workers themselves rather than to external shareholders. A further source of strength lies in workers’ practical knowledge of the labor process. Democratic firms give them both the means and the incentive to use that expertise to refine techniques and reorganize work. Innovations adopted through open deliberation gain legitimacy, and the direction of technological change is more likely to reflect workers’ interests than the capitalist bias toward control. But productivity alone cannot tell us whether work is well organized. Workers also care about the time and security they have outside the workplace and about how they are treated inside it. Those interests belong in any serious accounting of economic efficiency. Economic efficiency, properly defined, treats people’s preferences about the production process, working conditions, workload, job security, and more, on the same level as their consumption preferences. It is not necessarily an efficiency gain if a diner is able to provide coffee and lunch more cheaply while making its workers’ lives more precarious by quickly adjusting shifts according to demand. The gain to the customers comes at the expense of the security and income of the workers. There is, however, a tension between worker preferences and consumer preferences. In many cases, better satisfying worker preferences increases the cost of production or makes it harder for firms to adjust when demand changes. And though almost everyone is both a producer and consumer, the things we produce at work are only a tiny proportion of our own consumer basket. As a consumer, other people’s working conditions affect what we can afford. Other things (like quality) being equal, we normally choose a lower-priced product over a higher one, and even if we care about the conditions of production, we usually do not have much information about them. The increased flexibility of employment at the café benefits us directly, even if we would be much worse off if the same conditions prevailed in our own workplace. Workplace democracy structures people’s choices in ways that make it easier to reach a balance between our producer and consumer interests. It does this by democratizing decisions about work and pay. Unlike many consumption decisions, these are choices that are properly collective. In production, there are so many interdependencies between people’s preferences and formidable collective action problems in reaching generally preferred positions on the basis of individual bargaining. Because workers are also the residual claimants on firm profits, they can directly make decisions about any trade-offs between income and working conditions. To the extent that superior positions can be reached, with higher income and better conditions, democratic workplaces are better equipped to find them, given their advantages in morale, mutual monitoring, and likelihood of revealing information about labor processes in an environment of trust. Democratic firm management would not mean that producer preferences override everything else, because in a market socialist system firms must still take into account the preferences of their customers and generate enough revenue to cover their costs. Competing firms may make different choices about the pace of work, but they sell into the same markets, and no firm can charge higher prices simply to cover higher costs. The trade-off between higher income and a more leisurely pace of work is put directly to the workers in each workplace. For workers to exercise these choices, democratic firms need institutions that support them. If competition simply forces every workforce to cut its own pay and intensify its labor, formal control will offer too little freedom in practice. A national labor board could set wage and working-condition benchmarks, giving firms a common floor beneath which they could not compete. These benchmarks also help to spread gains from productivity growth to workers across the economy. Some sectors, especially in manufacturing, are more prone to labor-augmenting technological change than others, such as personal services. Central benchmarks help to make sure that the incomes of daycare workers, teachers, and hairdressers are not left lagging because gains from technological improvements are captured in industry. Investment would also need to be organized on different terms. Public banks could finance productive assets in partnership with democratic firms, so worker control would not depend on a workforce’s ability to buy out an owner with its own savings. Even many workers under capitalism who could pool together their savings in this way rationally choose not to do so, because it’s irrational to put all their financial eggs in the basket of a precarious new business venture. While defenders of capitalism might conclude that this makes capitalist labor contracts a mutually beneficial arrangement, we think no one should have to choose between economic insecurity and workplace despotism. Public banks can control enough eggs to spread them in a rational way throughout a number of baskets. Poorly performing firms will still be allowed to go under, but workers won’t lose their life savings when that happens. The democratic firm does not need to be an isolated cooperative struggling to survive in a hostile environment. It can be a basic cell of a larger, coherent system — one where social ownership, public banking, and market coordination work together to organize production efficiently and on democratic terms. When the Employers and Workmen Act passed in 1875, Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli claimed that for the first time in the country’s history, employer and employed “sit under equal laws.” Formally, that was true. Equality before the law meant that neither party could be jailed for breaking a civil contract. But it meant little else in a system where one class owned the means of production and the other was forced to work for them to survive. Today that most fundamental question of politics — that of self-determination and survival — remains unresolved. Workers already bear the consequences of decisions about production, investment, and the distribution of income. They deserve more than the freedom to protest those decisions. They deserve to be the ones to make them.

articles.title: Britain Used Modern Advertising to Sell Its Empire
articles.author: Owen Hatherley
articles.content: The American empire has never needed a propaganda ministry to justify itself to its subjects. For that, it has the world’s largest culture industry. From Hollywood to hip-hop, it has made millions around the world dream of being American, even those who hate its politics and economics. But American cultural imperialism comes into focus only when examined against its immediate precursor. For all the British Empire spread — constitutional monarchies, tea drinking, bleakly Protestant Christianity, and ruthless, amoral capitalism — it never made its victims aspire to be British in quite the same way as its American offshoot has. As for justifying itself at home: Who needs state propaganda campaigns when you have Call of Duty and Top Gun ? By contrast, in the twilight of their own imperial phase , the British set up a whole government body to sell their empire to consumers back home and to any unconvinced subjects abroad. It was called the Empire Marketing Board (EMB), a name that sounds hilariously quotidian to any English person of a certain age. While twentieth-century Britain also saw fit to establish state marketing boards for wool and milk, here the product was imperialism itself. The British Empire was once described by the liberal imperialist John Robert Seeley, in his 1883 bestseller The Expansion of England , as being the consequence of a series of what British liberals like to call “cock-ups.” He wrote, “We seem, as it were, to have conquered and peopled half the world in a fit of absence of mind.” Of course, even an apologist like Seeley didn’t believe that the wars, racial laws, and annexations that built the largest formal empire in history were accidental as such. What he meant was that the British Empire was disorganized. It was never, in fact, a unified state, politically or economically. But Seeley believed that it should be, so it could compete with the streamlined, industrialized, active United States and the German Empire, whose colonies were mostly contiguous and governed under the same laws (though here there were exceptions too, like Namibia and the Philippines ). The British Empire, according to Seeley, needed to be unified through tariffs and state planning. In the 1920s, this idea of an economically planned empire was briefly put into tentative practice by Britain’s Conservative governments, and the EMB was there to popularize it. The EMB produced posters, advertising campaigns, exhibitions, and documentary films. It was an unusual attempt to fuse two new trends in the interwar years: intensive advertising based on the American model and the propaganda of the Communist International . Its leading figure was an English bureaucrat, Sir Stephen Tallents, who had been convinced of the importance of art, cinema, and aesthetics after his time in Russia during its civil war. The British Empire sent troops to the Caucasus and the Baltic to help crush revolutionary socialism, and, in this capacity, the civil servant Tallents found himself the governor of Riga, the capital of Latvia and formerly a stronghold of Bolshevism. Looking at the agit-trains, kino tracts, and posters of the departed Soviets, Tallents realized that Britain was trailing far behind this powerful machine of persuasion. When Stanley Baldwin’s Tory government set up the EMB, Tallents was placed at its head. He in turn appointed as head of publicity one Frank Pick, the deputy director of the Underground Group, a private conglomerate that ran much of the capital’s public transportation network. A Fabian socialist who welcomed the London Underground’s nationalization in 1933 and a keen enthusiast for modern art, Pick subsequently brought in many of the artists he had worked with at the Underground. A good example is the 1926 poster by the British American artist E. McKnight Kauffer known as “Jungles Today Are Gold Mines Tomorrow,” referring to the slogan written at the top. The poster deployed the same bright, fauvist style Kauffer used elsewhere to convince London commuters to buy season tickets or move to the suburbs. It features two African figures, one male and one female, the woman in a traditional headdress holding aloft a pineapple, the man carrying a shield and staff; both have stylized features drawn in a manner that now looks distinctly racist. Between the two bodies is a ship and two columns of figures in pounds (goods sold and goods received, with the former mostly higher), indicating the increase in trade between Britain and its African colonies between 1895 — the start of the “Scramble for Africa” — and 1925. Other posters offered simple messages, presented in the neat serif fonts recently used in World War I propaganda. The most straightforward series asks you to buy the products of various colonies and white-settler dominions. BUY SOUTH AFRICAN ORANGES is emblazoned over a painting of gazelles, BUY CANADIAN HAMS AND BACON over one of a bison, and, more strangely, BUY BRITISH WEST INDIAN ST VINCENT ARROWROOT over an image of a turtle. Another campaign consisted of two posters, EAST AFRICAN TRANSPORT — OLD STYLE and EAST AFRICAN TRANSPORT — NEW STYLE. In the former, a group of Africans are marching with their livestock across the orange grass of a fauvist savannah. By contrast, the “new style” poster shows those same East Africans trading with a benevolent white man in a white shirt who occupies the high ground at the front of the scene. All of these designs expressed, queasily, Pick and Tallents’s idea of the empire as at once a modern network, linked by international transport, industry, and communications, and a warm, inclusive family in which everyone knows and works for one another, even the members in faraway parts of the globe (who are, of course, to be raised to full “adulthood” by the senior relations). EMB posters are seldom displayed today, for obvious reasons. But if it is largely forgotten in poster and industrial design, the board is much more significant in the history of British cinema. That’s because Tallents hired the Scottish sociologist, critic, and filmmaker John Grierson to head a specialized EMB Film Unit. The films Grierson produced, under the influence of Soviet directors like Dziga Vertov, are still considered classics, though their imperial provenance is not always emphasized. Many of the works of the British Documentary Film Movement that emerged in the late 1920s, such as Robert Flaherty’s Industrial Britain (1931), Basil Wright’s Song of Ceylon (1934), and Grierson’s own Drifters (1929), were all made for the EMB. It’s still possible to watch and enjoy The Song of Ceylon , a graceful, careful film that was intended to convince British filmgoers to drink Sri Lankan tea. The propaganda is subtle: the message that the balletic, elegant, rhythmic labor of the plantation workers resulted from the benevolence of empire is merely implicit. The Empire Marketing Board eventually came to an end not because it failed as propaganda but because the Tory government of the time was only partly committed to the project of imperial union. The notion of a unified trade bloc was fiercely opposed by the banks of London. The reason for this was that much of the formal empire, often acquired for military rather than economic reasons, was not particularly lucrative. On the other hand, the informal empire that would be placed on the other side of tariff walls — heavily British-influenced but officially nonimperial countries like Portugal, Iran, and Argentina — was extremely profitable. It may have fallen by the wayside, but perhaps some aspects of the EMB were unconsciously emulated in that vast, informal US empire after 1945 — not least a stress on the inestimable persuasive impact of cinema. What the EMB does offer, certainly, is a parallel. The project was created by an empire that knew it was under threat. Having grown rich and powerful on free trade, it now opted for tariffs, controlled markets under British supervision, and a planned industrial policy in order to beat its more technologically innovative competitors. These tactics didn’t work for Britain, and they seem unlikely to work for the declining United States now.

articles.title: JCTU Rent Strike
articles.author: Housing Justice Commission
articles.content: ETOC Cadre News: Jersey City tenants declare a rent strike at 5 separate buildings on the city’s west side FROM HUDSON COUNTY VIEW: Jersey City tenants declared a rent strike at five separate buildings on the city’s west side, alleging issues ranging from neglect, pests, and no on site building superintendent. “They just don’t care to fix anything. The kitchen floor is in awful shape. They put some screws in the kitchen floor tile so that they don’t move around too much. It’s an awful thing. We just gotta go on strike to get what we want,” Charlie, a tenant at 154 Belmont Ave. where a rally was held last week who declined to give his last name, said. “I’ve been living in this building 40 years. Nothing gets done, they want me to get out. Rats, mice, holes in the bottom, holes on top, and they still have the nerve to make me pay for water,” added fellow building tenant Luneste Alexender. 429 Bergen Ave., on rent strike since November, was joined this month by 150 and 154 Belmont Ave., also owned by Amir Ben-Yohanon. The Belmont buildings were previously without heat in the winter of 2024 along with 35 Kensington Ave., as HCV first reported . Ben-Yohanon owns these buildings through a separate LLC from 429 Bergen Ave., a common practice among Jersey City landlords who may have dozens of LLCs obscuring their real estate portfolio in the city. Tenants at 19 and 25 Kensington Ave. are also withholding rent from Optimum Properties. “I learned about this building a while ago but just recently I just learned the severity of how people are living here. I’m talking rats biting peoples’ toes, what looks like cracks in drooping walls,” Bergen Grand Tenants Association President Liv Malone declared at the rally. A tenant in the crowd interjected that the building at 429 Bergen Ave. has “water coming in everywhere.” “So I’ve just really enjoyed getting to know everyone who lives here and thinking about how they can get to live in a home that’s safe and that’s clean. Because I can promise you that the landlord that we share, Amir Ben-Yohanon, does not live like this and the only way that that will change is by the people living here deciding it’s done and that’s what you guys are doing here,” Malone concluded. Eli King, an organizer with Jersey City Tenants Union, echoed that sentiment without mentioning calling out any specific landlords. “Landlords know their power and they’re not afraid to use it, to neglect basic living standards in buildings they own to maximize the profit from their investment. Tenants are coming together and using our power: there’s more of us than there are of them and every dollar of those profits is money that we work for,” he asserted. “Both of these owners own massive portfolios in the city and we’re not going to stop with these buildings or with these landlords. Anyone who is ready to get organized and fight back against their landlord, come talk to us.” Ben-Yohanon did not return an email seeking comment on Sunday, while Optimum Properties could not be reached for comment.
