articles.title: Flicking the Switch on Flock
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content: Anonymously posing next to a Flock camera, advertising its links to ICE (Framingham Flock Coalition) By: Reid Jackson BOSTON – On September 16, Boston announced the end of its contract with Flock Safety after uncovering the company sharing local data with outside law enforcement. If this is shocking news to you, you may be a Boston City Councilmember: “Boston City Councilor Ben Weber said he was disappointed to see the agency was sharing data.” Boston is now the latest – and largest – city in New England to find out the hard way that Flock cameras are more trouble than they’re worth. The cancellation is the latest but not the first. While City Hall can be given a crumb of credit for doing the bare minimum and shelving the contract once the threat to data security became evident, it’s strange that the eight separate cases of cops misusing Flock cameras primarily to stalk former partners did not incentivize City Council to act. It’s also hard to excuse Flock violating the data sharing policy despite being strictly forbidden by the city’s contract: “When the Boston Police Department discovered that a Flock data-sharing function had been enabled despite a clear, contractual agreement prohibiting its use, BPD immediately directed the vendor to disable it,” the city and the Boston Police Department said in a joint statement on WCVB 5. “The city has since ended all use of Flock and will not use its services going forward.” The public can watch city officials and police run headfirst into its own crisis, considering the reputation of Automated License Plate Readers across the country. The public perception of state-approved spy cameras is exactly what you think it is , and according to some organizers in the Metrowest region, exactly the weapon that many fear. Bobbie, one Framingham resident and member of the Metrowest Neighborhood Group of the Boston chapter of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), has been present at every step of the process of the push to get Flock cameras not just removed, but outright banned in her town. The Metrowest area of Framingham and Marlborough has the largest population of Brazilian immigrants in the state , which has opened the towns up to become the main targets of ICE in the region. The movement to target surveillance technology arose from organizers within the LUCE Immigrant Justice Network of MA, after shifting from a focus on ICE verification training that characterized much of LUCE’s activity in 2025. Immigrant justice organizers were aware of ICE’s use of data from cameras like Flock’s to coordinate kidnappings. According to Bobbie: There was a lot of concern that ICE could have access to this technology to identify and kidnap our neighbors, and that the federal admin could use it to stalk activists. Plus, police forces from outside of Massachusetts could use it to track citizens looking for healthcare across state lines, which we had already seen proof of in 404 Media reporting. Bobbie said the first and most crucial step of their crusade against Framingham’s Flock program was to gather information, especially of the actual number of cameras in the city’s limits. This was a task that was only possible with the coordination of Framingham residents who mapped out everywhere they could find a camera on a city street, in order to accurately measure the success of the campaign. Framingham residents report using the website deflock.me to identify the cameras, as well as driving to each spot to visually confirm their location in town. Next was the ordinary avenues of public pressure on the local government. Despite the City Council’s sidestepping and shifting of responsibility between the police chief and the mayor, organizers successfully managed to land a date for a public hearing with a Flock official in Spring 2026 through a Framingham City Councilmember arranging a public forum to ask questions of a company representative. Coalition members held the representative’s feet to the fire as they attempted to dodge questions and explain away the infringements of residents’ civil liberties. Depending on the city leadership, campaigns here have two choices: extra pressure or public protest. Power-mapping is the strategic tool most helpful here, to determine the power relations unique to the municipality. Longer fought battles have been the case in similar campaigns against the much better funded data center projects such as the Dungeon in Lowell, which recently had its expansion paused by a state judge. Alternatively, in towns like Natick or Waltham, the town does not need an excuse to do away with a surveillance program . In Natick’s example, the project was not made known to the public or voted on by the Town Meeting or Select Board. Natick voted unanimously to end the program this February, and Waltham shut their cameras down just this month. For many of these towns, including Framingham’s removal of cameras this June, this marks only the first step. Since the state legislation is lagging behind this issue, municipalities are forced to set their own rules – and be pressured as organizing targets – for surveillance in their neighborhoods case-by-case. [When we started this campaign]… a few of our organizers initially thought we would only get regulation and not a full ban,” Bobbie said. “Even though we all wanted a ban… we learned we had more support on the full council for a full ban… after a ton of public comment from our organizers. Despite the reservations of more entrenched institutions, expanding the horizons of the politically possible is the organizers’ role. The fight against mass surveillance will be fought town-by-town, but with the help of a broad coalition like Mass 50501, Indivisible Mass Alliance, and DSA, the tools of one successful campaign can easily be repurposed for use in other towns, or in other fights against encroaching tyranny in the American empire. With Flock and other ALPR’s only becoming less and less popular, the tide is on the side of those fighting against accountability-free data collection. Reid Jackson is a member of the Metrowest Neighborhood Group of Boston DSA and contributing writer for Working Mass. NOTE: A previous version of this article misattributed LUCE as the source of reporting, when 404 Media was the actual source mentioned in-quote. This has been corrected in this version of this article. The post Flicking the Switch on Flock appeared first on Working Mass .

articles.title: Faith-Labor Organizing: Why Building Permanent Infrastructure is the Intervention This Moment Demands
articles.content: Featured image by Jared Rodriguez. Our congregations and our unions each have a measure of power. None of it is enough. The change we seek requires building power together; prioritizing building that power together in parallel with the work we are already doing alone. Our faith communities and labor unions share geographies, serve many of the same families, and claim a common commitment to human dignity. We rarely build power together. When we collaborate, the collaboration tends to be transactional: labor shows up for a rally the church organized, a pastor blesses a picket line. The event ends. Everyone goes home. No infrastructure remains. In Northern Virginia, our first Faith & Labor 2-day Training launched this April at Virginia Theological Seminary, a partnership between Virginians Organized for Interfaith Community Engagement , Virginia Theological Seminary and the Northern Virginia Labor Federation . The training brought together faith leaders, broad-based organizers and labor organizers into the same room to build shared infrastructure that outlasts any single campaign. Broad-based organizing offers labor something it cannot generate alone: deep relational practice, moral authority, and a base of power that reframes economic fights in terms that cut across partisan lines. A successful stop sign campaign at a dangerous intersection is a win. A collective bargaining contract at a single employer is a win. Neither builds the kind of power that can respond when a state agency is dismantled or when a national crisis demands coordinated action across regions. We need shared infrastructure: durable, adaptable, that can address systemic challenges affecting workers and their families, not just the local fights we can win alone. History is unambiguous: when worker rights and the moral arc of humanity advance most, faith communities and labor are in the trenches together. The abolitionist movement; the eight-hour workday; the sanitation worker strike in Memphis, where Martin Luther King Jr. died supporting a union strike. Civil rights and labor rights were never separate fights–they were the same fight, waged by people who understood that dignity is indivisible. When these movements separated, both weakened. Both institutions are losing members. Neither is losing infrastructure. Union halls still exist in every major metro area. Churches, mosques, and synagogues still anchor neighborhoods. When autocracy rises, it targets unions and prophetic religion, because organized workers and organized faith are the two forces that can mobilize people across race, geography, and class. Preventing a slide into autocracy requires these two traditions to be intentional and intentionality requires material investment in organizing money and people. It is also to recognize that the light at the end of the tunnel only becomes possible when labor and faith communities are joined tightly in the shared struggle for dignity. That history drove the partnership. But the immediate spark was simpler: we are organizing the same people separately, often for related fights, without knowing it. Three years ago, I began one-on-ones with labor leaders across Northern Virginia. The conversations revealed mutual frustration and mutual suspicion. Some union organizers saw faith communities as naïve, focused on charity rather than power. Some clergy saw labor as transactional, insufficiently concerned with the whole person and only looking to “rent a clergy” for rallies or strikes. Both sides had been burned by partnerships that felt extractive: show up for our event, lend us your credibility, then disappear. The breakthrough came when we stopped talking about collaboration and started practicing it. We plan to run joint listening sessions in congregations with a focus on speaking with private sector workers. We are in active practice of inviting labor organizers to observe our leadership development and vice versa–the traditions, while different, are not incompatible; they are complementary. A critical insight: each side must not feel the other is paternalistic or lecturing on how the other should organize. Labor has a century of hard-won wisdom about building power against adversaries with resources to crush you. Faith communities have centuries of practice holding people together through suffering, building the relational density that sustains movements across generations. We each have something to teach. We each have something to learn. The partnership only works if both sides believe that. Sixty million American workers say they would join a union if they could. Public approval of unions sits at 70 percent, near a sixty-year high. Meanwhile, union density continues to fall. The desire is there but the infrastructure to convert that desire into organized power is not. Church membership has fallen below 50 percent for the first time in Gallup’s history. Weekly attendance sits around 20 percent. Both institutions are losing members. Neither is losing infrastructure. Union halls still exist in every major metro area. Churches, mosques, and synagogues still anchor neighborhoods. What has eroded is the relational tissue between us, our leaders, and the communities we serve. Broad-based organizing offers labor something it cannot generate alone: deep relational practice, moral authority, and a base of power that reframes economic fights in terms that cut across partisan lines. Labor offers a rich history of disruptive power, grit, experience in the trenches, and organized workers with economic leverage that can translate moral witness into material wins. The planning process surfaced differences as expected. Language was the first negotiation. Labor organizers use “campaign” to mean a sustained, escalating fight with a clear target and timeline. Broad-based organizers use the word “campaign” more loosely than our labor counterparts do. For us, a campaign is the whole life cycle of an issue, not just the final push. That sounds like a small distinction until you try to build a strategy on top of it. We had to agree on the meaning of the words before we could agree on what to do. So we studied a fight that had already lived through that question, a worker led campaign over a public transit system in the City of Alexandria, Virginia, that showed us what solidarity between faith and labor actually looks like in practice. In 2018, drivers at DASH, the City of Alexandria’s public bus system, voted 97 to 13 to join Amalgamated Transit Union Local 689. DASH (unofficially known as Driving Alexandria Safely Home) is run as a nonprofit and staffs its workforce through a private company. The drivers earned less than nearby counterparts, and it took the drivers, prior to this campaign, over 20 years just to reach a top wage of $29 an hour. The fight had become a learning touchstone for the leaders gathered in April, trying to figure out how faith and labor can build together, because it served as an example of what it looks like to find solidarity between two sets of priorities. Pace is a point of divergence between broad-based organizing and labor organizing. Union campaigns run on tight deadlines. A contract expires, an election gets scheduled, management pushes back, and the deadline is non-negotiable. Broad-based organizing moves more consistently at the pace of trust, which can feel painfully slow to a colleague staring down a calendar but both have instances in which organizing conditions are interchangeable. Broad-based can have tight deadlines and labor can and does, at times, move at the pace of trust. The DASH fight shows the solidarity between the two, and it shows an example of a way forward. ATU had a hard date for a unionization election. But the foundation underneath that sprint was relational, and it was built one driver at a time. Organizers met drivers at the Subway down the street from the garage. They rode Metro dressed as passengers to talk with drivers off the clock. They learned that junior drivers had to be approached before senior drivers, who carried more resistance, and that reaching the Ethiopian drivers in the workforce meant bringing in someone those drivers already knew. When public pressure finally arrived, it landed on a base that had been built quietly for months. The sprint won the vote, 97 to 13. The trust made the sprint possible. We are still figuring out how to honor both rhythms, but DASH suggests we don’t have to choose. The surprises have been generative. Labor organizers were startled by how directly faith leaders talk about self-interest; not as selfishness but as the engine of sustainable commitment. Faith leaders were startled by how precisely labor organizers track power: who has it, who wants it, what they will do to keep it. The traditions are more compatible than either side assumed. VOICE is a founding affiliate of the Just Power Alliance, launched in 2024. The Alliance’s nine founding affiliates represent roughly 330 institutions and organize over half a million people across the East Coast, Mid-Atlantic, and Great Lakes. After Virginia, the model could scale across the network: DC, Maryland, Boston, Milwaukee, Cleveland, Connecticut. Each geographic location is anchored in local faith-labor partnerships. The vision is not a new national organization. It is national infrastructure; organizers and leaders in different cities, fluent in the same skills and in more than one organizing tradition, who can support one another’s campaigns and develop leaders who move between the sanctuary and the union hall. Organized money benefits from the division between faith and labor. When we fight housing battles without labor’s economic leverage, we lose. When we fight contract battles without faith communities’ moral authority, we fight alone. The structural separation between our movements is not inevitable. It is a condition we can organize against. If you are an organizer, a pastor, a rabbi, an imam, a union leader, or a lay leader, the question is whether you will prioritize building power with people outside your institution along with the work you are already doing inside it. If you believe the change you seek requires building the power to achieve it, your answer should be yes.

articles.title: Trump’s Greenland Deal Puts His Annexation Plans on Ice
articles.author: Huw Paige
articles.content: Donald Trump recently concluded an agreement with the governments of Greenland and Denmark over the status of the Arctic island. Trump presented it as a big victory for his efforts, claiming that it granted the United States “permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many US concerns.” The substance of the agreement told a different story. After doing lasting damage to the relationship between the United States and Europe, the Trump administration got more or less the same deal it could have obtained by asking politely. Trump’s repeatedly stated plan to acquire Greenland has been put on the back burner. End of the Saga? “Greenland belongs to the Greenlanders — it cannot be taken from us,” Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens Frederik Nielsen proclaimed in a Facebook post that showed him grinning contentedly. A saga that has brought hitherto unprecedented attention to his country seemed to be coming to an end. The deal , signed by the leaders of Greenland, Denmark, and the United States at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, permits the US to open two bases in Greenland, Mestersvig in the east and Narsarsuaq in the south. Mestersvig is a base for the Sirius Patrol, a dogsled unit of the Danish military operating in the remote Northeast Greenland National Park. Narsarsuaq is an airfield that was constructed during the World War II as a US airbase and that closed as an international airport earlier this year. A recent investigation by the Danish newspaper Politiken found that when the Americans left most of their Greenlandic bases after finding Cold War replacements for them, they abandoned “several thousand tons of hazardous or contaminated waste.” At Narsarsuaq, this waste material included oil drums and asbestos sheets scattered around the old base. The Trump administration has presented this outcome as a vindication of its strategy. But the United States has long been able to construct new facilities in Greenland if it has the consent of the other parties. The 1951 Defense of Greenland Agreement , reached after the US had taken responsibility for Greenland’s security during Denmark’s wartime occupation, established this principle. The negotiations that have proceeded in earnest since the start of 2026 could have happened without any US threats to take control of the island. “Sensitive Sectors” However, the new agreement does contain several changes in other areas. Whereas the 1951 agreement was valid for as long as NATO existed, the new version, officially intending to “amend and supplement” the old one, stresses its permanence and includes provisions for a future independent Greenland. At the same time, it requires that an independent Greenland “agree to remain in NATO, including by applying to become a member if necessary.” This suggests that some commentary inspired by the absence of any reference to NATO in Trump’s post was slightly overblown. In other respects, the deal formalizes an unwritten understanding that investment in “sensitive sectors or activities” by non-NATO states is unwelcome. This understanding was already clear during the first Trump administration, when Denmark provided funding for Greenlandic airport upgrades to avoid a hostile US reaction over potential Chinese investment in the project. Back in 2016, Denmark rejected a Chinese bid to take over the Kangilinnguit naval base due to “security concerns.” China’s much-vaunted Arctic ambitions have been constrained in recent years. While the exact meaning of the term “sensitive” is open to debate, the US seems to have obtained an effective veto over any future Russian or Chinese presence in Greenland. Questions also remain elsewhere: the agreement does not address the question of resource extraction in Greenland (apart from a clause that prohibits “control” or “strong influence” by non-NATO states and investors, unless the parties agree that their activities “would not constitute a threat to national security or public order”). Trump’s threats prompted the formation of a unity government after the last election, with four of the five parties in the Greenlandic parliament taking part before one withdrew earlier this year. This means that policy differences between its constituent parties over this question have been left unresolved. Demokraatit, the party of Greenland’s prime minister, Jens Frederik Nielsen, is in favor of extraction, while Inuit Ataqatigiit, the party of his foreign minister, Múte Egede, takes a different stance. It won the 2021 Greenlandic election on a platform of opposition to a uranium and rare earth mining project in the country’s south. Disputes between the Greenlandic government and a US oil firm with links to Trump have sporadically flared up over the question of which licenses it needs and whether the licenses it already has access to are valid. If these disputes drag on into next summer, and Trump-friendly figures within Greenland Energy get the president’s ear, things could erupt again. An agreement on security does not preclude a later dispute on other issues, especially where there is money to be made. White Gold Rush Although some elements of the deal could prove consequential, its most significant part may well be the opening preamble. For the first time in the relationship between Greenland and the United States, this is an agreement negotiated from the outset by a Greenlandic government. In January 2026, two Inuit scholars released a briefing paper on the ongoing impact of colonization on Greenland. Vivi Vold and Kunuk (Sandra) Inutiq highlighted Washington’s “imperialist and colonialist” rhetoric but stressed that Denmark could not “demand silence” on other topics in the name of unity against the United States. Two of the cases that they mentioned bear repeating here. First, disgraceful episodes such as the implantation of IUDs into thousands of Inuit women and girls between the 1960s and the 1980s, many of whom did not give their consent, remain unresolved. Rival reports were released in August this year, after a group of four experts could not agree on a verdict. The report released by the Greenlandic government suggested that the term “genocide,” which Múte Egede had used during his time as prime minister, could not be ruled out. The other report, produced by two of the experts who split from the government-backed group, reached a less strident conclusion. Neither report had a Greenlandic Inuit coauthor. Second, mining of the mineral cryolite, which is important for the production of aluminium, generated vast amounts of wealth for Denmark in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. As it happens, the naval base China unsuccessfully sought to purchase in 2016 was originally constructed by the US Navy to protect the very same cryolite mine. In Greenland, American influence is never far away. There was a fierce controversy in Denmark after the public service broadcaster DR released a documentary called Greenland’s White Gold in the buildup to the 2025 Greenlandic election. The documentary attempted to calculate the scale of this windfall and suggested that it may have amounted to 400 billion kroner in today’s money. By making this calculation, the program makers sought to push back against a persistent Danish idea that Denmark’s contribution to the Greenlandic government budget is akin to a generous gift. An economist who had appeared in the documentary questioned one of its core calculations, and the Danish culture minister strongly criticized it. After initially standing by the program, DR pulled it from its streaming service, and a senior editor resigned. The fact that an issue like this could flare up at the height of the “Greenland crisis” reveals the deep feelings that persist within what many still view as a colonial relationship. US posturing has disrupted Denmark’s gradual acknowledgment of its history with Greenland, allowing the former colonizer to portray itself as a protective elder sibling. No Good Colonizers The standoff has also diverted attention from other domestic issues. In May 2025, local hotel owner Mike Nicolaisen organized a protest against the lack of investment in Tasiilaq, the largest settlement on Greenland’s east coast. Six hundred people — one-third of the town’s population and nearly a sixth of the entire region’s inhabitants — showed up. Nicolaisen and his wife, Anette, subsequently announced the formation of a new “Party for an Independent East Greenland.” In an interview with KNR, Greenland’s national broadcaster, he described the protest as a “cry for help” and said that the aspirant party was necessary to bring attention to his region: “The only time we’re remembered is when it’s about suicide, misery, and alcohol.” Decades of underinvestment in the regions and a lack of employment opportunities has drawn people to move either to the capital, Nuuk, or to Copenhagen. Population growth in Nuuk has kept house prices extremely high, combined with slow construction rates and the difficulty of finding empty land on the rocky peninsula upon which the city is situated. There is also a significant problem of homelessness. The Greenlandic government cannot trust that this new deal will permanently satisfy the United States. But skilful negotiation by the Danish and Greenlandic governments has avoided a doomsday scenario. Trump is now claiming a win at little cost to his negotiating partners, and arguments over resource extraction have been deferred. Now that the specter of Greenland’s potential seizure by force has been put to bed for the time being, there is more space for reckoning with the ongoing legacies of colonization, which can help prevent the formation of new relationships based on similar premises. Trump may have brought Denmark and Greenland closer together, but there is still no such thing as a better colonizer.
